title: China Shock 2.0: Key Messages
gist: Capital Economics' Neil Shearing sums up its China Shock 2.0 series: Beijing's export surge is a deliberate, durable strategy, larger and more technologically advanced than the 2000s shock, hitting Europe hardest, widening global imbalances and risking a financial crisis absent policy change in Beijing or Washington.

insights.claim: China's export surge is the product of deliberate policy aimed at technological self-sufficiency while making the rest of the world more dependent on Chinese production; the domestic costs of excess capacity and weak demand are tolerable to Beijing.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Do not assume China will change course because it hurts at home; expect export push to persist for several years.

insights.claim: Slower economic growth together with rising export competitiveness is not a contradiction but a defining feature of China Shock 2.0, and China is likely to keep gaining market share from advanced economies despite its structural slowdown.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Continued disinflation in goods and share loss for developed-economy manufacturers.

insights.claim: China now accounts for just under one-fifth of global goods exports versus just over 5% in the early 2000s, so the rest of the world is much more exposed.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Scale amplifies spillovers versus the first shock.

insights.claim: Chinese firms now compete at the technological frontier in electric vehicles, batteries, robotics and AI rather than low-cost manufacturing, and do so against a more fractured geopolitical backdrop where Washington sees China as a strategic rival.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: High-productivity sectors are at risk, and adjustment will be harder than before.

insights.claim: China's excess capacity is a disinflationary force that Capital Economics estimates will reduce global inflation by around 0.1-0.2 percentage points over the coming years.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Supports lower goods inflation and central-bank room, offsetting some oil-driven pressure.

insights.claim: Production relocating away from China creates opportunities elsewhere, particularly in South East Asia, with Vietnam a prominent beneficiary and Malaysia also gaining.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics

insights.claim: China Shock 2.0 could reduce euro-zone GDP growth by around 0.1-0.2 percentage points a year, with Germany hit harder, bringing large manufacturing job losses and stronger support for populist parties.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: European industrials and politics are the most exposed channel; expect industrial-policy responses.

insights.claim: Economic nationalism and active industrial policy are likely to be lasting features of the political landscape over the next decade, and governments and firms will weight security and resilience above pure efficiency.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for reshoring, defence-adjacent and resilience capex.

insights.claim: China's current account surplus has risen to a record relative to global GDP because its production-over-consumption model has not been matched by imports; the mirror deficit is largest in the US, where the source is now the public-sector deficit rather than private borrowing.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Links China Shock 2.0 directly to US fiscal sustainability concerns.

insights.claim: Capital Economics estimates the renminbi is undervalued by around 25% in real terms, but a stronger renminbi alone would deepen Chinese deflation without stimulus to domestic demand, and US deficit reduction would be needed too.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: A CNY revaluation is not a standalone fix; it requires a coordinated package.

insights.claim: A modern 'Plaza Accord' would be the best resolution, but coordinated adjustment is highly unlikely between strategic rivals, so imbalances will most likely keep building and raise the risk of some form of crisis.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Tail risk of a disorderly adjustment in FX, bonds or trade; hedge accordingly.
